note: Matthew copies Mark closely (over 70% of his words), but notice the harvest numbers. Mark's yield climbs, {mk 4:8 ἓν τριάκοντα καὶ ἓν ἑξήκοντα καὶ ἓν ἑκατόν} (“thirty, sixty, a hundred”). Matthew reverses it: {mt 13:8 ὃ μὲν ἑκατὸν ὃ δὲ ἑξήκοντα ὃ δὲ τριάκοντα} (“a hundred, sixty, thirty”). Luke keeps only the top figure, {lk 8:8 ἑκατονταπλασίονα} (“a hundredfold”). A hundredfold was an extraordinary harvest, the kind Isaac reaped when God blessed him (Genesis 26:12).

Mark's wording is startling: parables are given to outsiders {mk 4:12 ἵνα βλέποντες βλέπωσι καὶ μὴ ἴδωσιν} (“**so that** seeing they may see and not perceive”), {mk 4:12 μήποτε ἐπιστρέψωσιν} (“lest they turn”). Matthew changes the purpose into a cause: {mt 13:13 ὅτι βλέποντες οὐ βλέπουσιν} (“**because** seeing they do not see”). Matthew and Luke both make Mark's singular “mystery” plural, {lk 8:10 γνῶναι τὰ μυστήρια} (“to know the mysteries”), a minor agreement.

Mark has Jesus scold the disciples first: {mk 4:13 Οὐκ οἴδατε τὴν παραβολὴν ταύτην} (“don't you understand this parable?”). Matthew drops the rebuke, as he usually protects the disciples. Each Gospel names the bird that steals the seed differently: Mark's {mk 4:15 ὁ Σατανᾶς}, Matthew's {mt 13:19 ὁ πονηρὸς} (“the evil one”), Luke's devil. Luke also gives the key in a single line: {lk 8:11 Ὁ σπόρος ἐστὶν ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ} (“the seed is the word of God”).

A cluster of short proverbs that Mark strings together here and Matthew scatters across his Gospel (5:15, 7:2, 10:26, 13:12). The lamp under {mk 4:21 τὸν μόδιον} (*modios*, a grain-measuring bucket) uses a Latin loanword, one of several in Mark. Mark's {mk 4:24 ἐν ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖτε μετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν} (“with the measure you measure it will be measured to you”) appears in the Sermon about judging in Matthew and Luke.

The only parable found in Mark alone. The farmer sleeps and rises while the seed grows {mk 4:27 ὡς οὐκ οἶδεν αὐτός} (“he does not know how”), because {mk 4:28 αὐτομάτη ἡ γῆ καρποφορεῖ} (“the earth bears fruit **by itself**”, *automatē*, the source of “automatic”). Matthew and Luke both omit it. Matthew may have replaced it with his parable of the wheat and the weeds, which also features a sleeping sower and a harvest.

Only Matthew has this parable. An enemy sows {mt 13:25 ζιζάνια} (*zizania*, usually identified as darnel, a weed that looks like wheat until it ripens) among the grain. The master forbids weeding: {mt 13:30 ἄφετε συναυξάνεσθαι ἀμφότερα μέχρι τοῦ θερισμοῦ} (“let both grow together until the harvest”). It speaks to a mixed community waiting for a final judgment, a recurring concern in Matthew.

Mark says the seed is {mk 4:31 μικρότερον ὂν πάντων τῶν σπερμάτων} (“the smallest of all seeds”), a proverbial claim, and that it becomes {mk 4:32 μεῖζον πάντων τῶν λαχάνων} (“the greatest of all garden plants”). Matthew and Luke **both** say it becomes a {lk 13:19 δένδρον} (“tree”), one of the minor agreements. Luke's version stands closer to Matthew's than to Mark's, so Two-Source scholars think Matthew blended Mark with a Q version. The birds nesting in its branches echo Daniel 4 and Ezekiel 17.

Nearly word for word in both, including the exact quantity {mt 13:33 ἀλεύρου σάτα τρία} (“three *sata* of flour”), roughly 40 litres, enough bread for a hundred people. Sarah bakes the same amount for angelic guests in Genesis 18:6. The woman {mt 13:33 ἐνέκρυψεν} (“hid”) the leaven, an odd verb for baking. Leaven is usually an image of corruption in the Bible, which makes the parable even more striking.

Mark's summary adds that in private {mk 4:34 τοῖς ἰδίοις μαθηταῖς ἐπέλυεν πάντα} (“he explained everything to his own disciples”). Matthew turns it into a fulfillment of {mt 13:35 Ἀνοίξω ἐν παραβολαῖς τὸ στόμα μου} (“I will open my mouth in parables”). That is Psalm 78:2, which Matthew attributes to “the prophet”; the psalm is credited to Asaph, called a seer in 2 Chronicles 29:30. Some manuscripts even read “Isaiah the prophet”.

Matthew's allegorical key for his own parable: {mt 13:38 ὁ δὲ ἀγρός ἐστιν ὁ κόσμος} (“the field is the world”). The finale borrows the furnace from Daniel 3 and a phrase Matthew loves: {mt 13:42 ὁ κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὁ βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων} (“weeping and gnashing of teeth”). It appears six times in Matthew and once in Luke. Its interest in final separation is typical of Matthew's Gospel.

Three short parables found only in Matthew. The man who finds treasure sells everything {mt 13:44 ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς αὐτοῦ} (“out of his **joy**”). The section ends with a riddle that many readers take as the evangelist's self-portrait: {mt 13:52 πᾶς γραμματεὺς μαθητευθεὶς τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν} (“every scribe trained for the kingdom”) brings out of his storeroom things new and old.

Each Gospel phrases Peter's confession differently. Mark: {mk 8:29 Σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστός} (“you are the Christ”). Luke: {lk 9:20 Τὸν χριστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ} (“God's Christ”). Matthew: {mt 16:16 ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος} (“the Son of the living God”). Only Matthew adds the blessing on Peter, with its pun {mt 16:18 σὺ εἶ Πέτρος καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ} (“you are *Petros*, and on this *petra*”). John's version: {jn 6:69 σὺ εἶ ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ} (“the Holy One of God”).

The turning point of Mark. Jesus says it is necessary ({mk 8:31 δεῖ}) for the Son of Man to suffer and rise {mk 8:31 μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας} (“**after** three days”). Matthew and Luke both change this to {lk 9:22 τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ} (“**on the third** day”), matching the creed-like wording of 1 Corinthians 15:4. Matthew gives Peter actual words, {mt 16:22 Ἵλεώς σοι κύριε}, roughly “God forbid, Lord!” Luke omits Peter's protest and the “Satan” rebuke entirely.

Among the highest agreement anywhere in the Synoptics: nearly 80% of Matthew's words here are Mark's. Luke adds one word that turns martyrdom into a way of life: take up the cross {lk 9:23 καθ ἡμέραν} (“**daily**”). Mark's closing promise, that some will see {mk 9:1 τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐληλυθυῖαν ἐν δυνάμει} (“the kingdom come in power”), becomes in Matthew seeing {mt 16:28 τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐρχόμενον ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ} (“the Son of Man coming in his kingdom”).

Mark and Matthew use the verb {mk 9:2 μετεμορφώθη} (“was **metamorphosed**”). Luke avoids it, perhaps because it sounded like pagan myths of gods changing form, and writes {lk 9:29 τὸ εἶδος τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ ἕτερον} (“the appearance of his face became different”). Matthew's {mt 17:2 ἔλαμψεν τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ὡς ὁ ἥλιος} recalls Moses' shining face. Only Luke reports the conversation: Moses and Elijah spoke of {lk 9:31 τὴν ἔξοδον αὐτοῦ} (“his *exodus*”) in Jerusalem.

Mark's Jesus answers cryptically: {mk 9:13 Ἠλίας ἐλήλυθεν καὶ ἐποίησαν αὐτῷ ὅσα ἤθελον} (“Elijah **has** come, and they did to him whatever they wished”). He never names him. Matthew makes it explicit, as he often does: {mt 17:13 τότε συνῆκαν οἱ μαθηταὶ ὅτι περὶ Ἰωάννου τοῦ βαπτιστοῦ} (“then the disciples understood he meant John the Baptist”). In Matthew the disciples understand; in Mark they rarely do. Luke omits the conversation.

Mark's version is twice as long and contains a famous line only he has: {mk 9:24 Πιστεύω βοήθει μου τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ} (“I believe; help my **unbelief**”). Mark's Jesus says this kind comes out only {mk 9:29 ἐν προσευχῇ} (“by prayer”). Later manuscripts add “and fasting”. Matthew blames the disciples' {mt 17:20 ὀλιγοπιστίαν} (“little faith”, one of his favorite words) and describes the boy as {mt 17:15 σεληνιάζεται} (“moonstruck”), the ancient term behind “lunatic”.

All three record the disciples' reaction differently. Mark: {mk 9:32 οἱ δὲ ἠγνόουν τὸ ῥῆμα καὶ ἐφοβοῦντο} (“they did not understand, and were afraid to ask”). Luke keeps this, but explains that the meaning {lk 9:45 ἦν παρακεκαλυμμένον ἀπ αὐτῶν} (“was concealed from them”), as if God had hidden it. Matthew replaces the incomprehension with grief: {mt 17:23 ἐλυπήθησαν σφόδρα} (“they were greatly distressed”), so his disciples understand all too well.

Only Matthew has this story. Jesus pays the annual temple tax with a coin found in a fish's mouth: {mt 17:27 εὑρήσεις στατῆρα} (“you will find a *stater*”), a four-drachma coin, exactly the half-shekel tax for two people. After the temple's destruction in 70 CE, Rome diverted this tax to the temple of Jupiter in Rome, which may explain why Matthew's community cared about whether and why to pay it {mt 17:27 ἵνα δὲ μὴ σκανδαλίσωμεν αὐτούς} (“so as not to offend them”).

The disciples argue about who is greatest right after the passion prediction, and in each Gospel the answer turns on a child. Mark's rule: {mk 9:35 Εἴ τις θέλει πρῶτος εἶναι ἔσται πάντων ἔσχατος} (“whoever wants to be first must be last of all”). Matthew sharpens it into a condition of entry: {mt 18:3 ἐὰν μὴ στραφῆτε καὶ γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία} (“unless you turn and become like children”). Luke: {lk 9:48 ὁ γὰρ μικρότερος ἐν πᾶσιν ὑμῖν} (“the least among you all”) is great.

The only time Mark gives John a line on his own: {mk 9:38 εἴδομέν τινα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί σου ἐκβάλλοντα δαιμόνια} (“we saw someone casting out demons in your name”). Jesus' answer, {mk 9:40 ὃς γὰρ οὐκ ἔστιν καθ ἡμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐστιν} (“whoever is not against us is for us”), seems to clash with the Q saying “whoever is not with me is against me”. Matthew, who has that saying (12:30), omits this story; Luke keeps both.

Mark's millstone is a {mk 9:42 μύλος ὀνικὸς} (“a **donkey** millstone”), the huge upper stone turned by an animal, not the small hand mill. Luke has a different wording, {lk 17:2 λίθος μυλικὸς}, in a different context. Mark closes with Isaiah 66:24, {mk 9:48 ὅπου ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτᾷ} (“where their worm does not die”). Later manuscripts repeat this line twice more, as verses 44 and 46, which most modern Bibles now omit.

The same parable with two different applications. In Matthew the sheep {mt 18:12 πλανηθῇ} (“**wanders off**”), and the point is pastoral care in the church: it is not the Father's will that {mt 18:14 ἀπόληται ἓν τῶν μικρῶν τούτων} (“one of these little ones be lost”). In Luke it is {lk 15:4 ἀπολέσας} (“**lost**”), and the point is heaven's joy over {lk 15:7 ἑνὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ μετανοοῦντι} (“one sinner who repents”), answering critics of Jesus' company.

Matthew turns a short saying into a procedure for discipline, ending {mt 18:17 εἰπὸν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ} (“tell it to the church”). *Ekklēsia* appears in the Gospels only here and in 16:18. Then forgiveness without limit: {mt 18:22 ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά} can mean “seventy-seven times” or “seventy times seven”. It is the Septuagint phrase of Lamech's boast of unlimited **revenge** (Genesis 4:24), reversed. Luke has {lk 17:4 ἑπτάκις τῆς ἡμέρας} (“seven times a day”).

Only Matthew tells this parable, and its numbers are deliberately absurd. The first servant owes {mt 18:24 μυρίων ταλάντων} (“ten thousand talents”). *Myrioi* is the largest Greek number word, and a talent was about 6,000 days' wages, so the debt is beyond any lifetime of work. His fellow servant owes him {mt 18:28 ἑκατὸν δηνάρια} (“a hundred denarii”), about three months' wages. The ratio is roughly 600,000 to one.
